idiom_name: hand-rolled reduce over frozen Data states with an observer list (no MVI framework)
implementation_notes: Ruby's mainstream stack is server-rendered HTML: Rails renders a page and Turbo/Stimulus replace fragments from the server, so there is no client-side view layer to drive with intents and no consumer for the loop. Data.define (Ruby 3.2+) can express immutable value states and case/in pattern matching can express a reducer, but the state holder, dispatch and subscription are all hand-written, objects are mutable by default, and per-request state belongs in the controller or session rather than a long-lived state holder. Where a Ruby process genuinely holds presentation state (TUI tools, long-lived service consoles), an events bus (dry-events, Wisper, ActiveSupport::Notifications) plus scoped state is the idiomatic substitute; the classic MVI structure is justified only for a small, fully hand-rolled state class in such a process.
code_sketch:
State = Data.define(:items, :loading, :error)

def reduce(state, intent) # intent: {type:, ...} or a Data object
  case intent
  in {type: :refresh}        then State[state.items, true, nil]
  in {type: :loaded, items:} then State[items, false, nil]
  in {type: :failed, error:} then State[state.items, false, error]
  else state
  end
end
# holder: @state = reduce(@state, intent); @observers.each { |o| o.call(@state) }
pitfalls: Objects are mutable by default and Data freezes only the top level; a nested Array in a state still changes a previous snapshot.
A global state holder in a threaded server (Puma, Sidekiq) is shared across requests and leaks one user's screen state into another's; keep it per-request or per-session.
Observer callbacks registered from request-scoped objects outlive the request and keep stale objects referenced; unsubscribe or use the framework's event bus.
Rebinding a constant (STATE = reduce(STATE, intent)) warns and can shadow the original; hold the state in a mutable container object instead.
alternative: Keep the one-way flow server-side: the request is the intent, the controller/service updates the model and re-renders, and Rails with Hotwire (Turbo/Stimulus) supplies the HTML-over-the-wire loop; use dry-events or Wisper for in-process fan-out. If a client-side reducer loop is genuinely required, implement it in the JavaScript layer where a declarative view and the reducer tooling exist.
